# ChainLog benchmark results

**Generated by `bench/run.sh`. Do not edit by hand.** Every number below
came from a program in `bench/`, run on the machine described here.
Regenerate with:

```bash
make bench
```

Medians over **5 runs**, with the full range shown so the spread is
visible. Medians rather than means: one unlucky run moves a mean and
barely moves a median.

| commit | `dd0375b` |
| CPU | Apple M3 (8 cores) |

| arch | arm64 |

| filesystem | APFS |

Built at `-O2`, no sanitizers. The test build uses ASan and UBSan, which
roughly halve throughput; benchmarking that would measure the sanitizer.

## SHA-256 throughput

| implementation | MB/s (median) | range |
|---|---|---|
| ChainLog, hand-written | **345** | 330 – 347 |
| `shasum -a 256` | 413 | |
| `openssl dgst -sha256` | 2133 | |

Hashing 128 MiB in 64 KiB chunks. The `openssl` figure includes
process startup and file I/O, so it understates the library slightly.

This is the honest cost of the project's main constraint. `openssl` uses
the ARMv8 cryptographic extensions -- single instructions for the SHA-256
round function -- and this implementation does not. The gap is the price
of writing it by hand, and it is the right trade for a project whose
purpose is understanding the construction.

## Append throughput

| sync policy | appends/s (median) | range | µs each |
|---|---|---|---|
| `every` (default, 3 fsyncs) | **164** | 163 – 167 | 6081 |
| `batch:100` | 15428 | 15358 – 15574 | |
| `batch:1000` | 29129 | 28177 – 31447 | |
| `none` | 42017 | 39400 – 42536 | 23.8 |

100-byte records. `every` measured over 500 appends per run
(it is slow enough that more would add minutes); the others over
100000. The final `flush()` is inside the measured window for
every policy, so a batched run is not flattered by work it had not done
yet.

**What this is actually measuring.** The default policy issues three
`fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC)` calls per append -- one for the write-ahead log, one
for the main log, one after clearing the WAL. At 6081 µs
per append that is roughly 2.0 ms
per barrier, which is the drive being asked to flush its own write cache.
Plain `fsync()` on APFS does not do that, which is why this project uses
`F_FULLFSYNC` and why the number looks the way it does.

Peak RSS for an append run: **1.8 MiB**, independent of
record count -- appending is O(1) in memory apart from the pending
block's hashes.

## Verify

| records | log size | open (s) | verify (s) | range | records/s | MB/s | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100000 | 19.1 MiB | 0.0522 | **0.1664** | 0.1651 – 0.1706 | 601108 | 115 | 2.3 MiB |
| 1000000 | 190.7 MiB | 0.5275 | **1.72** | 1.67 – 1.74 | 582743 | 111 | 2.3 MiB |

`open` and `verify` are separated because they do different work.
`open` walks every frame checking the magic, the lengths and the CRC-32
but computes no SHA-256. `verify` recomputes every record hash, every
chain link and every Merkle root. The difference is the hashing.

**Peak RSS does not grow with the log.** Verify streams frames and holds
only the current block's leaf hashes -- 1024 x 32 bytes at the default
block size, so 32 KiB regardless of whether the log has a thousand
records or a million. That is the one design decision in the project that
shows up directly as a measured number.

The 1000000-record corpus was built with `--sync none` in
25.0 s. At the default policy it would have taken about
101 minutes,
which is itself a useful illustration of what the barriers cost.

## Merkle trees and proofs

| leaves | levels | build (s) | proof steps | proof on the wire | proof+verify (µs) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 | 11 | 0.0012 | 10 | 360 B | **7.36** |
| 1048576 | 21 | 0.6328 | 20 | 690 B | **8.87** |

1024 leaves is the real case: it is the default block size, so it is the
tree an inclusion proof is actually built over. 1048576 leaves is
there because the brief asks for it, and because it shows the shape of
the curve.

**The proof grew from 10 steps to 20 for a tree
1024x larger.** That is the O(log n) claim as a measurement rather
than an assertion: 10 doublings of the leaf count added
10 hashes. On the wire a proof for the 1048576-leaf tree is
690 bytes, including the 26-byte self-describing header and the
4-byte CRC-32.

Build peak RSS at 1048576 leaves was 97.5 MiB, of
which 33.3 MiB is the leaf array itself. The tree
holds every level, so it is roughly 2n nodes. At the default block size
of 1024 this is 1.5 MiB and entirely uninteresting; the
large figure is the cost of the benchmark's unrealistic tree, not of the
log.

## Not measured

Stated explicitly so nothing here is read as covering it:

- **Concurrent readers and writers.** The lock serialises writers and
  nothing has been measured under contention.
- **Cold cache.** Every verify run above reads a file the OS has just
  written, so the figures are warm-cache. A cold read would be bounded by
  the device, not by hashing.
- **Spinning disks, network filesystems, or any machine but this one.**
  `F_FULLFSYNC` costs are hardware-specific and these numbers do not
  transfer.
- **`prove` on a large log.** `prove` walks the log from the start to
  reach a block, which is O(records before it); only the in-memory tree
  work is measured above.
- **HMAC signing overhead on append.** One MAC per sealed block is far
  below the noise floor of a single fsync, so it was not isolated.
